info.name: Baileys API v0.4
info.description:
REST API for WhatsApp, built on Baileys.

- **58 requests** across 6 folders.
- Set `base_url`, `session` and `apikey` in the collection variables before sending anything.
- Every response uses the same envelope: `{ success, message, data }`.
- Bodies are JSON. Form-encoded bodies are accepted too, but JSON is what the
  examples use.

### Authentication

The `apikey` is only checked when `AUTHENTICATION_GLOBAL_AUTH_TOKEN` is set on
the server; with it unset, everything is open. It is read from either the
`apikey` header or the `apikey` query parameter, and this collection sends it as
a query parameter using the `apikey` variable.

### Errors every route can answer with

| Code | Message | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `401` | `Authentication failed.` | The `apikey` does not match, and a token is configured. |
| `400` | `Please fill out all required input.` | A field the route requires was missing or empty. |
| `404` | `Session not found.` | The `id` does not match a session. |
| `400` | `There is no connection with whatsapp at the moment, please try again` | The session exists but its socket is not open. Not raised on `/sessions/*`, which has to work while a session is connecting. |

### A note on `isGroup`

Several bodies contain `"isGroup": {{isGroup}}` — **deliberately unquoted**, so
Postman substitutes the boolean `false`. If you edit one of these, keep it a real
boolean. Sending the string `"false"` is truthy on the server, which would treat a
private chat as a group and produce a `@g.us` JID.

Source: https://github.com/andresayac/baileys-api

item.name: Sessions

variable.description: Your created session id.

request.description:
Confirms that a session id is known to the server.

`sessionValidator` answers `404` for an unknown id, so a `200` here only means
the id exists. It says nothing about whether the session is logged in or
connected, and the response carries no payload (`data` is `{}`).

variable.description: Your created session id.
Your created session id.
Your created session id.

request.description:
Connection state of a session.

| `status` | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `authenticated` | Connected **and** logged in — the only state that can send |
| `connected` | Socket is open, but the login has not finished (a QR may still be waiting) |
| `connecting` | Socket is opening |
| `disconnecting` | Socket is closing |
| `disconnected` | Socket is closed |
| `unknown` | A socket state the API does not recognise |

`connected` is not a synonym for ready: a session sitting on an unscanned QR
reports `connected` and cannot send anything.

variable.description: Your created session id.

request.description:
Every session id the server currently holds, as a plain array of strings.

The entries are ids, not objects, and there is no connection state here — call
`GET /sessions/status/:id` for that.

A session is listed as soon as `POST /sessions/add` registers it, which is
before it has been scanned, so an id can appear while it is still waiting for a
QR.

Create a session and start logging in.

The session id comes from the **body**, not the query.

`typeAuth` selects how you authenticate:

| Value | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| `qr` | The response is held open until a QR code is ready, then returns it as a base64 data URL. This is the default. |
| `code` | Sends a pairing code to `phoneNumber` instead, and returns it as `code`. |

To use a pairing code, send `{ "id": "my-session", "typeAuth": "code", "phoneNumber": "628123456789" }`.
`phoneNumber` is required when `typeAuth` is `code` and ignored otherwise.

The response to `qr` is held open until the code is ready, so allow for the
round trip. **The QR is delivered exactly once** — if it is not scanned before
WhatsApp rotates it (about a minute), the session logs itself out and is deleted,
and you have to call this endpoint again. See the README's *Session Lifecycle*
section.

A session id that is already in use answers `409`.

variable.description: Your created session id.

request.description:
Log the session out and delete it, credentials and message store included.

The session must exist (`404` otherwise). Queued scheduler jobs are deleted with
it — they belong to a session that no longer exists and could never be sent.

item.description:
One example per message type. All of them post to `POST /chats/send`; only the `message` object changes.

Any of them also accepts `typing` to show a typing indicator first — see **Send Message**.

request.description:
Private chats known to the session.

Read from the in-memory store rather than from WhatsApp, so it returns
immediately and only contains what this session has seen since it was created.
Each entry is a Baileys chat object — `id`, `name`, `unreadCount`,
`conversationTimestamp` and so on.

Group chats live in `GET /groups`.

query.description: id field from message key used as cursor to fetch previous messages (Optional).
fromMe field from message key used as cursor to fetch previous messages. Value: 'true' or 'false', default: 'false' (Optional).

variable.description: The group jid, or the chat jid.

request.description:
Message history of a chat, newest first.

Paging is **backwards from a known message id**:

| Query | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `limit` | How many messages to return. Default `25`. |
| `cursorId` | A message id from this chat; the results are the messages older than it. |
| `cursorFromMe` | `true` / `false` — the `fromMe` flag of that same cursor message. Needed whenever `cursorId` is set, because an id on its own is ambiguous: a message you sent and one you received can share an id. |
| `isGroup` | `true` when `jid` is a group. Defaults to `false`. |

To fetch the next page, take the last message of the current one and send its
`key.id` as `cursorId` and its `key.fromMe` as `cursorFromMe`.

The names are **camelCase**. An unrecognised query parameter is ignored rather
than rejected, so `cursor_id` would not error — it would silently hand you the
newest page again.

query.description: id from any message key used as cursor to fetch previous messages (Optional).

variable.description: Chat jid.

query.description: id from any message key used as cursor to fetch previous messages (Optional).

variable.description: Chat jid.

request.description:
Forward a stored message into another chat.

`forward.id` and `forward.remoteJid` identify a message **in this session's own
store** — the API forwards the copy it holds, not one re-fetched from WhatsApp.
A message that is not in the store answers `404`, so read the conversation first
if you are not sure.

`receiver` is the destination and `isGroup` selects group handling for it.

response.name: Response Success

request.description:
Download the media attached to a stored message.

`remoteJid` and `messageId` identify a message in this session's store, so the
message has to have been received by this session first.

`404` when the message is not in the store, `500` when it carries no media or
the download fails.

response.name: Response Failed

request.description:
Send a message to a phone number or a group.

`message` is passed to Baileys untouched, so every message type is supported here
— text, image, video, audio, document, sticker, contact, location, poll and react.
The dedicated examples under **Send Message Types** show the shape of each.

`isGroup` selects group JID handling for `receiver`.

### Typing indicator

Add `typing` to show "typing…" before the message is delivered.

| Value | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| `true` | Derive a duration from the length of the message text |
| `1500` | Show it for 1500 ms |
| `{ "duration": 1500 }` | Same thing |
| `false`, `0`, `""` | No indicator — the default when omitted |

The indicator is always cleared before the message is sent, and a socket that
refuses to show it will not stop the message going out.

response.name: Response Success

request.description:
Revoke a message for everyone in the chat.

`message` is the message **key** — `remoteJid`, `fromMe`, `id` — not the message
content. It revokes your own messages; revoking somebody else's fails.

`500` when WhatsApp refuses, which is what happens if the message is too old or
was not sent by this session.

Tell a chat whether you are online, offline, typing, and so on.

Presence can be one of the following:

- `unavailable`
- `available`
- `composing`
- `recording`
- `paused`

`isGroup` selects group handling for `receiver`.

`composing` is what a typing indicator is. The `typing` option on the send
endpoints does this for you and clears it again — see **Send Message**.

Mark messages as read, clearing their unread badge for this session.

`keys` is an array of message keys, and at least one must carry an `id`.

For a group message include `participant`, the JID of whoever sent it — without
it WhatsApp cannot tell which message you mean.

item.name: Contacts
item.description: Look up whether a phone number, LID or username exists on WhatsApp, and resolve between the three.

request.description:
Check whether phone numbers, LIDs and usernames exist on WhatsApp.

All three fields are optional, but at least one is required. Each is an array and
each is reported back **separately**, because they answer different questions: a
number lookup wants its LID back, a LID lookup wants the phone number behind it,
and a username lookup wants the JID.

- **`lid` is the only way to learn the number ↔ LID mapping.** LIDs are opaque,
  so nothing about them can be derived. A number with no published LID reports
  `lid: null`; it still exists.
- **A LID lookup answers with the phone number in `jid`** — the reverse mapping.
  That is why the two lists are not merged.
- **`contact`** says whether the account is a saved contact of the session, not
  whether the username exists.
- Unknown values come back with `exists: false`, in the same order you sent them.
- Numbers are normalised, so `+62 811 111 1111` and `628111111111` match. A value
  with no digits at all is rejected with `400`.
- Long lists are batched 50 users per USync query.

The session must be **logged in**; an unscanned QR session is refused with `400`
rather than left to wait out the query timeout.

response.name: Response Success

item.name: Groups

request.description:
Group chats known to the session.

Read from the in-memory store, so each entry holds only what a chat list holds —
id, name, unread count, timestamps. **No participant lists.**

For the members, use **Group List With Participants**, which asks WhatsApp
directly.

fromMe field from message key used as cursor to fetch previous messages. Value: 'true' or 'false', default: 'false' (Optional).

request.description:
Message history of a group, newest first.

Same paging contract as `GET /chats/:jid`, minus `isGroup` — the `jid` of this
route is always a group.

| Query | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `limit` | How many messages to return. Default `25`. |
| `cursorId` | A message id from this group; the results are the messages older than it. |
| `cursorFromMe` | The `fromMe` flag of that same cursor message. |

The names are **camelCase** — `cursorId`, not `cursor_id`. An unrecognised query
parameter is ignored rather than rejected.

Change who may edit the group and who may post.

| `announcement` | Only admins may send messages |
| `not_announcement` | Everyone may send messages |

| `unlocked` | Everyone may edit the group info |

request.description:
Set the group's profile picture from a public image URL.

The URL must be reachable by the server, not just by you. `400` when the group
does not exist or the session is not a participant.

Every group the session participates in, **with** its participant list.

Unlike `GET /groups`, which answers from the in-memory store, this asks WhatsApp
directly: slower, but current. Use it when you need the members, and `GET /groups`
when you only need the chat list.

Renamed from "Group List Without Participants", which described the opposite of
what this does.

item.name: Scheduler
item.description:
Queue messages to be sent later, optionally repeating. Jobs are held in memory and mirrored to `sessions/scheduler.json`, and re-armed on boot.

Only `POST /scheduler` needs a live WhatsApp connection — a job queued for a
socket that cannot send would just burn through its retry budget. The other four
routes deliberately use a weaker session check and keep working while a session
is reconnecting.

A failed attempt is retried up to `SCHEDULER_MAX_ATTEMPTS` times, waiting
`SCHEDULER_RETRY_DELAY` between tries. Exhausting the budget marks the job
`failed`; it is never dropped silently.

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `pending` | Waiting, waiting to retry, or an unfinished series waiting for its slot |
| `sent` | A one-off handed to WhatsApp |
| `completed` | A repeating job that ran its full `count`, or passed its `until` |
| `failed` | Every attempt failed; `lastError` says why |
| `cancelled` | Cancelled before it ran |
| `missed` | A one-off whose time passed while the process was down past the grace window |

request.description:
Queue a message to be sent later.

`scheduledAt` accepts an epoch millisecond number, a numeric string, or an ISO
8601 date string, and must be in the future.

`message` is passed to Baileys untouched, so anything `POST /chats/send` accepts
works here too. `typing` behaves exactly as it does there.

`scheduledAt` is what you asked for; `runAt` is when it will actually run. They
differ once a job has been retried.

request.description:
Queue a message that repeats.

`every` accepts `hourly` / `daily` / `weekly`, a duration string (`30s`, `15m`,
`2h`, `1d`) or a number of milliseconds. Anything under 1000 ms is rejected —
that is a loop, not a schedule. A bare string works as shorthand:
`"repeat": "daily"`.

Two optional limits sit alongside it:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `count` | Total sends, the first one included. Omit for unlimited. |
| `until` | Last time an occurrence may run. Omit for no end. |

`runs` counts the occurrences actually delivered, so it doubles as the cursor
into the series. The job stays `pending` between sends and becomes `completed`
only when `count` is used up or the next slot would fall past `until`.

Worth knowing:

- **The cadence is anchored to `scheduledAt`, not to the last send**, so a slow
  send or a retry does not push every later occurrence back.
- **Occurrences missed while the process was down are skipped, not queued up.** A
  week of downtime on a `daily` job resumes at the next slot instead of firing
  seven messages at once.
- **A missed series survives a restart.** Unlike a one-off, which becomes

originalRequest.description:
Queue a message that repeats.

`every` accepts `hourly` / `daily` / `weekly`, a duration string (`30s`, `15m`,
`2h`, `1d`) or a number of milliseconds. Anything under 1000 ms is rejected —
that is a loop, not a schedule. A bare string works as shorthand:
`"repeat": "daily"`.

Two optional limits sit alongside it:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `count` | Total sends, the first one included. Omit for unlimited. |
| `until` | Last time an occurrence may run. Omit for no end. |

`runs` counts the occurrences actually delivered, so it doubles as the cursor
into the series. The job stays `pending` between sends and becomes `completed`
only when `count` is used up or the next slot would fall past `until`.

Worth knowing:

- **The cadence is anchored to `scheduledAt`, not to the last send**, so a slow
  send or a retry does not push every later occurrence back.
- **Occurrences missed while the process was down are skipped, not queued up.** A
  week of downtime on a `daily` job resumes at the next slot instead of firing
  seven messages at once.
- **A missed series survives a restart.** Unlike a one-off, which becomes
  `missed`, a repeating job is moved to its next slot and stays `pending`.
- **Rescheduling restarts the series.** `PUT /scheduler/update/:jobId` with a new
  `scheduledAt` resets `runs` to `0`.
- **A failed occurrence burns the job, not the series.** If every attempt fails
  the job ends as `failed`; revive it with `PUT /scheduler/update/:jobId`.
